transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

Well, thank you so much for seeing me, doctor. I really appreciate your time. I, um, I hope I'm not wasting it. 

It's just... well, my mind just doesn't seem to want to hold onto things anymore. I'm sure it's probably just a normal part of getting a bit older, but... well, I sit down to write a simple note for the youth maker program I help out with. It's something I could do in my sleep before, you know? But lately, the numbers and the words, they just... they scatter on me. I just can't seem to pull them together. 

I know that probably sounds a bit silly, doesn't it? I hope that's the right kind of thing to bring up.

When you say your mind doesn’t hold onto things anymore, does this include forgetting things that happened recently, like what you did earlier today, or mostly things you used to know well, like familiar tasks or names?

Oh, gosh... I'm sorry, doctor, I'm not entirely sure how to answer that. I hope it's alright that I don't have a very clear picture of it. 

I haven't really noticed a specific pattern, to be honest. I don't think I'm forgetting what I did earlier today—or, well, I suppose I could be and just haven't caught it, but nothing too drastic, I don't think. I really don't want to give you the wrong information. 

It just feels more like... when I try to focus on doing something, the thoughts just sort of slip away before I can use them. I'm so sorry I can't be more specific for you. Does that make sense at all, or would you like me to try and keep a better record of it for next time?
Have you noticed any trouble remembering something you just learned, like a new name or a phone number someone told you a few minutes ago?

Oh, let me think... no, I don't believe so. I always try to make a point of repeating a new name when I hear it, just to be polite, you know? And that seems to be working just fine. Same with phone numbers, if someone tells me one, I can still hold onto it long enough to jot it down. 

I really hope I'm not making things harder for you by saying no to that. I know you're trying to put the pieces together, and I want to be as helpful as I can. I just haven't noticed any real issues with the new things like that. Is it okay that I don't have trouble with that part? I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need.
Have you been having trouble focusing or keeping your attention on tasks, like following a conversation or reading something?

Yes, doctor, I think that's exactly it. I... I'm so sorry, I probably didn't do a very good job explaining it when we first sat down. But that's precisely what I meant earlier about trying to write those notes for the youth program. 

When I sit down and try to focus on them, or read through the materials, my attention just won't stay put. Like I was saying, the words and the numbers just scatter on me, and I can't seem to keep my mind fixed on the task at hand. It's just so frustrating because I want to do a good job for them. 

I hope it's alright that I brought that same example up again. I really don't want to sound like a broken record, I just want to make sure I'm answering you properly. Is that the sort of thing you were asking about?
Have you been feeling down, sad, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy lately?

Oh, well... I, um... I really hate to complain, doctor. I know I have a lot to be thankful for, and I don't want to sound ungrateful or... or like a burden. 

But, yes... I suppose I have been feeling quite down lately. Most days, I wake up with this... this heavy, almost hollow feeling right here in my chest. And it just sort of stays with me. Even when my wife is right there, talking so kindly to me—she's so wonderful, really, I don't want you to think she's doing anything wrong—but even then, I just feel like I'm... like I'm sitting at the bottom of a deep well, and I just can't reach the top. 

I'm sorry, that sounds so dramatic, doesn't it? I really don't mean to make a fuss about it. I just... I hope I'm explaining it okay. Is that the kind of thing you need to know? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right answers.
Have you found that things you used to enjoy, like hobbies or time with family, don’t bring you the same pleasure they used to?

Well, um... I really don't want to sound like I'm giving up on things, because I know it's important to stay active. I try, I really do. But... I suppose, if I'm being completely honest, things just haven't held the same appeal lately. 

Like my woodworking... I have some really nice wood pieces just sitting on my bench right now, and I haven't even touched them. And I've been skipping the choir planning meetings, and my chess games too. Even fishing... normally I'd jump at the chance to get out on the water, but lately, it just sounds like more effort than it's worth. Which really isn't like me at all. 

I feel terrible admitting that, especially when the choir and my friends count on me. I hope I don't sound lazy or... or like I'm just making excuses. I'm still trying my best, I promise. Does that make sense? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture without sounding too negative.
Have you noticed a decrease in your energy level or felt unusually tired, even when you haven’t been doing much?

Well, um... I wouldn't say I've been unusually tired, exactly. I mean, at my age, you know, you can't expect to have the energy of a young man anymore. I try to stay busy when I can, and I certainly don't want to come across as someone who just sits around all day doing nothing. 

I suppose maybe I've been taking a few more rests than usual, but nothing too out of the ordinary, I don't think. I really try to push through it so I'm not a bother to my wife. I don't want her worrying about me being lethargic or anything like that. 

I hope that's an okay answer. I just don't think I've noticed a major drop in my energy, all things considered. Is that what you were looking for?
Would you say that you no longer enjoy activities that used to bring you happiness or satisfaction, like woodworking, choir meetings, or spending time with family?

Oh, um... well, I know we just touched on this a moment ago, and I really hope I didn't give the impression that I'm completely miserable or... or ungrateful for the things I have. I know I mentioned the woodworking and the choir and... and everything. 

I suppose... yes, it's just that the spark isn't quite there right now. I don't want you to think I've stopped caring about my family, though! I still love spending time with them, I really do. It's just... I guess the joy I usually feel is a bit... muted? 

I'm sorry to repeat myself, I just want to be sure I'm answering you properly. I don't want to sound like a broken record or like I'm just complaining. Am I giving you the right kind of information? I really want to be helpful.
Have you found that you take little or no pleasure in most or all activities, even the ones you used to enjoy the most?

Oh, my... I feel terrible, Doctor. I know you've asked me something very similar just a moment ago, and I really hope I'm not frustrating you or giving you the wrong answers. I want to be as helpful as possible, I promise. 

But... yes, I suppose it really is most things right now. Like I mentioned before, I just haven't touched the wood pieces sitting on my bench, and I've been skipping the choir planning and my chess games. Even fishing... it just sounds like more effort than it's worth these days, which really isn't like me at all. 

I hate admitting that because I don't want to sound like a complainer or like I'm just giving up. I really am trying. Is that... is that the kind of information you need? I just want to make sure I'm doing this right and giving you what you need for your notes.
Have these feelings of sadness and loss of interest been present most of the day, nearly every day, since this started?

Well, um... I really hope I'm not painting a picture of someone who just sits around moping all day. I try my best to put on a brave face, especially for my wife. I don't want to bring her down, you know? 

But, I suppose... if I'm being completely honest, and I want to be honest with you... yes, it does feel like it's there most of the time. Even when I'm trying to stay busy or keep a smile on, that heavy feeling just sort of lingers in the background, pretty much every day lately. 

I really try not to let it show, though. I hope that makes sense? I just want to make sure I'm explaining it the right way for you.
How long have you been feeling this way, with the sadness and loss of interest in activities?

Oh, well... I really don't want you to think I'm just wallowing, Doctor. I know people go through hard things all the time and handle them just fine. I really am trying to push through it. 

But, um... I guess it's been about three weeks now. It, well... it started right around the time my older sister passed away. I know I shouldn't be letting it affect me this much, and I'm really trying to get back to normal. I just... I haven't quite bounced back yet. 

I hope it's okay that I mentioned that? I don't want to overshare or make excuses, I just thought it might be important for you to know when it all started. Am I giving you the right details?
You mentioned feeling this way for about three weeks. Have your symptoms been present for most of the day, nearly every day, during this time?

Oh, um... yes, Doctor. I know I just said that, and I'm so sorry if I'm making you repeat yourself. I really don't mean to be difficult or make your job harder. 

But yes, it's been pretty constant for those three weeks. Like I said, I really do try to stay positive and keep busy, so I hope it doesn't sound like I'm just letting it take over my whole day. I am fighting it, I promise. But... yes, the heavy feeling is there most of the day, almost every day since she passed. 

Is that... is that helpful? I just want to make sure I'm answering exactly what you're asking.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight recently—like eating more or less than usual, or losing or gaining weight without trying?

Well, um... I really hate to admit this, because my wife goes to the trouble of making wonderful meals and I'd hate for you to think I'm ungrateful. I really do try to eat, I promise. But... I suppose food has mostly just lost its appeal for me lately. 

I don't want you to think I'm doing it on purpose, but I end up just sort of... pushing my breakfast around the plate. And then, well, by the time supper rolls around, my wife is usually reminding me that I've barely eaten anything all day. I feel terrible making her worry about it, and I'm really trying to do better for her. 

I hope it's okay that I explained it that way? Does that answer your question, Doctor?
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or feeling restless and unable to sit still lately?

Oh, um... well, I really hope I'm not making myself sound worse than I am. I know I'm getting a bit older, being 67 and all, so I suppose some of it might just be my age catching up with me. I don't want you to think I'm just sitting around letting myself go. 

But... my wife has mentioned that I seem a bit sluggish lately. I hate to admit it, but she's right. It just feels like everything takes so much more effort. Even just getting out of my favorite chair, or... or trying to find the right words to answer you right now. It's almost like my body and my tongue are moving through wet cement. I really am trying to keep up my usual pace, I promise. I don't want to be a burden to anyone. 

Does that make sense, Doctor? I hope I'm not complaining too much. I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.

inference_history.note: Initial presentation of cognitive difficulties, possible memory issues, and concern for age-related changes. Differential includes mild cognitive impairment, early dementia, depression-related cognitive symptoms, and normal age-related changes.

The patient reported symptoms of depression (persistent sadness, loss of interest, feelings of hopelessness), which rules out cognitive disorders (F04, G30.9) and most likely mild cognitive impairment (F06.8). The depressive symptoms support keeping F32.9 (major depressive episode) and F33.9 (recurrent depressive disorder). F48.1 (dysthymia) remains possible but less clearly supported. No single disorder is yet definitive.

The patient endorsed symptoms of depressed mood and anhedonia, which are key features of depressive disorders. This makes F48.1 (Dysthymia) less likely compared to major depressive episode (F32.9) or recurrent depressive episode (F33.9).

The patient has reported symptoms of sadness, loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities, difficulty concentrating, and persistent symptoms for the past three weeks following a bereavement. These symptoms are present most of the day, nearly every day. While the symptoms meet criteria for a major depressive episode, the duration is less than two years and there is a clear precipitant (sister’s death), making both F32.9 (Major Depressive Disorder, single episode, unspecified) and F33.9 (Recurrent Depressive Disorder, unspecified) possible. The distinction between a single episode and recurrence cannot be determined without more historical information.

The patient described symptoms consistent with a major depressive episode, including persistent sadness, loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities, and difficulty concentrating. These symptoms have been present for about three weeks, nearly every day and most of the day. There is also a noted decrease in appetite. While this could suggest a diagnosis of a single major depressive episode (F32.9), the duration of symptoms is still slightly short of the minimum duration typically required for a formal diagnosis (at least two weeks), and it is unclear whether the symptoms represent a first-time episode or a recurrence. Therefore, no further narrowing from F32.9 and F33.9 is warranted at this time.
